background.definition: Speech delay represents a heterogenous group of disorders without a clear or consistent definition. A child is considered to have speech delay if his or her speech is significantly below developmental norms for the child's age. This group of disorders includes expressive and receptive language delay, as well as disorders of language (syntax, phonology, pragmatics, and so forth), stuttering, and articulation disorders. See .

list.listitem: Prevalence estimates vary widely according to inclusion criteria, with various studies reporting prevalence rates ranging from 2.3% to 19%.
For children aged 2.0 to 4.5 years, prevalence of combined speech and language delay is between 5% and 8%.
Preschool-aged children with speech and language delay may be at an increased risk for learning disabilities and lower academic achievement once they reach school age.
Children who have speech delay at primary school entry may be at risk for emotional, behavioral, and social problems in later childhood and adolescence.
Primary—cannot be accounted for by any other condition
Autism
Mental retardation
Cerebral palsy
Hearing impairment
Global developmental delay
Cleft lip and palate
Social deprivation or neglect (including internationally adopted children)
Constitutional (maturational) delay
Exact pathophysiology is unknown. Brain imaging studies of children with speech delay have failed to show any anatomic correlate.
Genetic factors may play a major role, but as of yet no consistent genetic markers have been established.
Deficits in processing of auditory stimuli and immature synaptic connections have been theorized as possible contributing factors.

There is insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of the universal use of brief, formal screening instruments to detect speech and language delay or disorders in children up to 5 years of age. B
Universal newborn hearing screening does not appear to be helpful in preventing speech delay. B

Although there are several formal screening instruments that have sensitivity and specificity above 80%, there is no clear consensus on the optimal ages and frequency for screening. There also is no clear evidence that early screening and intervention for speech delay result in long-term improvements in nonspeech and language outcomes.

In a small cohort study, extremely preterm infants (EGA less than 28 weeks at birth) of Hispanic and African-American ethnicity were at higher risk of developing expressive and receptive speech delay. Also, a systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that children born before 37 weeks' gestation had lower scores than term-born children on simple and complex language tests, even after controlling for major disabilities and socioeconomic status. The implications for these findings for screening in the general population are unknown.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force concluded that there is insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of routine use of brief, formal screening instruments to detect speech and language delay in children up to 5 years of age.

The efficacy of universal newborn hearing screening to improve long-term language outcomes also is uncertain. One systematic review estimated that 6771 newborns would have to be screened for hearing loss to prevent 1 additional case of delayed language acquisition.
Refer children younger than 3 years with suspected speech delay to a local Early Intervention Program or a speech-language pathologist for formal speech assessment. C
Refer all children with suspected speech delay for a formal audiologic evaluation to rule out hearing loss. C

Speech and language development should be measured against expected milestones at all well child care visits as part of routine developmental surveillance (). Speech and language can be assessed by formal screening instruments, by physician inquiry, or by parental questionnaires.

The presence of certain developmental red flags should prompt immediate referral for a formal speech evaluation (see ). Certain non-verbal items, such as lack of response to name, lack of gesturing or imitation, and lack of object or symbolic (pretend) play, also can be warning signs of significant speech delay.
Parental concerns about delayed speech and language development should always be taken seriously.

Although family history of speech delay and perinatal factors (preterm delivery, low birth weight) are associated with a higher risk of speech delay, there is no evidence to support enhanced surveillance for children with such risk factors.

There is no gold standard test for the screening or diagnosis of speech delay in the primary care setting. Several brief screening instruments that can be administered in the office setting are available, but the sensitivity and specificity of these instruments varies widely (sensitivity: 17%-100%; specificity: 45%-100%).

When speech delay is suspected in a child younger than 3 years, the child should be referred to an Early Intervention Program or to a speech-language pathologist for formal speech evaluation (Figure 1).
As an alternative, children who are mildly behind in their speech development can be closely observed for a period of 3 months prior to referral.
All children with suspected speech delay should be referred for a formal audiologic evaluation to rule out hearing loss.

Since speech delay may be the initial presentation of autism or pervasive/global developmental delays, any child that is confirmed to have speech delay should undergo formal assessment of other developmental domains (gross and fine motor, adaptive, social, and so forth).
Speech therapy should be individualized to the child's specific speech and language deficits, and should include parent training. C
Speech therapy is effective for phonological and expressive vocabulary difficulties, but is less effective for receptive language delays. A
Prompt insertion of tympanostomy tubes in children with otitis media with effusion or persistent middle ear effusion is not helpful in preventing speech and language delay. A
Children who stutter should be referred to a speech-language pathologist who specializes in the Lidcombe Program. B

In children with a history of persistent otitis media with effusion, prompt insertion versus delayed insertion of tympanostomy tubes does not result in improved speech or language acquisition at 4 years of age.
In a follow-up study, delayed insertion of tympanostomy tubes did not result in abnormal speech development at 9 to 11 years of age.
Children with a confirmed diagnosis of speech delay should receive speech therapy that is tailored and individualized to their specific speech and language deficits.

Individual speech therapy may be more useful initially to help establish the structural aspects of language, while group interventions are useful in facilitating generalization of language skills to other settings. However, current data suggests that there is no significant difference in outcome between individual and group interventions.
Speech and language therapy is effective in the short term for children with phonological and expressive vocabulary difficulties.
There is less evidence that interventions for children with receptive language difficulties are effective, and the evidence for interventions targeted at expressive syntax difficulties is mixed.
Speech interventions delivered by clinicians and by trained parents are equally effective, and the use of normal language peers as part of therapy is beneficial.

The Lidcombe Program, in which parents under the direction of a speech pathologist provide verbal behavioral feedback to children who stutter, is effective in markedly decreasing stuttering in children.

Parent training should be included as part of any formal speech intervention. Training should include information on expected speech milestones, as well as methods of facilitating language development and generalizing speech to natural settings.

Currently there is insufficient data to determine the optimal timing, duration, or intensity of speech therapy. Limited data suggests that interventions lasting longer than eight weeks may be more effective.
Children with speech and language delay who do not receive therapy are at risk of having their speech delays persist into school-age years. B
Children with continued speech delay at entry to school have an increased incidence of social difficulties and attention problems as adolescents. B
One systematic review found that up to 60% of speech or language delays may resolve spontaneously without treatment between the ages of 2 and 3 years.
However, the same review also found that between 41% and 75% of children diagnosed with early expressive language delay continued to have reading problems at 8 years of age.
Children with receptive language delay generally have a poorer prognosis and are at greater risk of residual speech delay.
Short-term prognosis for children who receive speech therapy for primary speech and language delay is generally good.
Speech therapy has been reported to improve toddler socialization skills, child self-esteem, and play behavior. However, there is a paucity of data on long-term prognoses.
One cohort study reported that in children who continued to have language delay at age 5.5 years, there was an increased incidence of social difficulties and attention problems at age 15 years.

feature.caption: Categories of Speech and Language Delay.
feature.feature_body:
Articulation The production of speech sounds
Dysfluency Interrupted flow of speech sounds, such as stuttering
Expressive language The use of language to share thoughts, comment, or protest
Language The conceptual processing of communication, which may be receptive, expressive, or both
Morphology The rules governing meanings of word units
Phonology The set of rules for sound production
Pragmatics Adaptation of language to the social context
Prosody Appropriate intonation, rate, rhythm, and loudness of speech utterances
Receptive language Understanding of language
Semantics A set of words known to a person that are part of a specific language (vocabulary)
Speech Verbal production of language
Syntax The way linguistic elements are put together to form phrases or clauses (grammar)
Voice disorders Difficulty with speech sound production, usually at the level of the larynx. May be related to motor or anatomical issues.
Adapted from Nelson HD, Nygren P, Walker M, Panoshca R. Screening for speech and language delay in preschool children: systematic evidence review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. Pediatrics 2006;117:e298-e319.

feature.caption: Speech and Language Developmental Milestones.
feature.feature_body:
6 mo Babbling
Turns toward voice
9-10 mo Imitates speech sounds
Says "dada" or "mama" without meaning
12 mo Says "dada" or "mama" with meaning plus 1 other word
Plays "pat-a-cake" or waves "bye-bye"
Responds to "no"
15 mo Says "dada" or "mama" plus 3 other words
Indicates wants by pointing or gestures (not crying)
Follows 1-step command
18 mo Vocabulary of 10-20 words
Points to 1 or 2 body parts
Extensive/mature jargoning
24 mo Vocabulary of at least 30-50 words
Combines 2 words
Follows 2-step command
30 mo Uses 3-word sentences (subject, verb, object)
Names at least 1 animal picture
Uses pronouns appropriately
36 mo Uses 3- to 5-word sentences, plurals, and past tense
Names 4 animal pictures, counts 3 objects correctly
Vocabulary of 250-400 words
Speech 80% intelligible
Adapted from Leung AK, Kao CP. Evaluation and management of the child with speech delay. Am Fam Physician 1999;59:3121-3128. City Health Information (Vol. 20, No. 3): Developmental Delay in Young Children. New York: New York City Department of Health, 2001. Nelson W, Behrman R, Kliegman R, Marvin A, eds. Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics. 15th ed. Philadelphia: WB Saunders, 1996:41, 44.

feature.caption: Developmental Red Flags Suggesting Need for Immediate Speech and Language Evaluation.
feature.feature_body:
By 12 mo No babbling, pointing, or gestures
By 15-16 mo Not using any single words
Does not look at or point to objects or people named by the parents (lack of joint attention)
By 18 mo Not using "Mama," "Dada," or other names
Does not follow 1-step commands
By 24 mo No spontaneous 2-word phrases
Vocabulary less than 20 words
Does not point to pictures or body parts when named
By 30 mo Does not respond to questions (either verbally or by nodding/shaking head)
By 36 mo Does not follow 2-step commands
Vocabulary less than 200 words
Does not ask for things by name
Persistent echolalia to questions
At any age Regression or loss of previously acquired speech milestones
Data from Prater CD, Zylstra RG. Autism: a medical primer. Am Fam Physician 2002;66:1667-1674. Schum RL. Language screening in the pediatric office setting. Pediatr Clin North Am 2007;54:425-436.
